stem:
A 6-year-old boy has had an intermittent itchy, dry scaly rash for a number of years. It is usually worse in the dry winter months and can flare after swimming in a pool. His parents keep it under control with a regular moisturiser and a mild topical corticosteroid. Both his parents suffer from hay fever and his older sister has episodic asthma.

He presents to the emergency department with a 7-day history of a progressively worsening rash consisting of crusted, yellow weeping plaques. He has a fever of 37.8°C and the rash is very pruritic. This is different from his usual rash, and moisturisers have not helped.

Which of the following is the most appropriate next step in management?

options.text: He needs to be commenced on intravenous immunoglobulin
Perform bacterial swabs and commence him on empirical antibiotics
Treat the patient and the entire family with topical permethrin
Urgently arrange for allergic skin prick testing

explanation: This child has atopic dermatitis with likely secondary bacterial infection (impetiginised eczema), suggested by yellow crusting, weeping plaques and low-grade fever. The appropriate management is to take bacterial swabs if needed and start empirical antibiotics. IVIG, permethrin and allergy testing are not indicated here.

optionExplanations.A: IVIG is not a treatment for infected eczema or impetigo.
optionExplanations.B: Correct — this is consistent with bacterial superinfection of eczema, so swabs and empirical antibiotics are appropriate.
optionExplanations.C: Permethrin treats scabies, which is not the best fit for this presentation.
optionExplanations.D: Skin prick testing is not an urgent management step for an acutely infected rash.
